method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: **Mucous membrane irritation and GI symptoms usually come first, then CNS depression**, which raises the risk of aspiration pneumonitis.
claims.source_text: Mucous membrane irritation and gastrointestinal symptoms usually develop first, followed by CNS depression which increases the risk of aspiration pneumonitis
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Essential_Oil_Poisoning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Aspiration risk comes from the oil and from added hydrocarbons or emulsifiers.** Symptoms are oil-specific — **call Poisons Information if the oil is known (13 11 26).**
claims.source_text: Aspiration pneumonitis is a risk from both the essential oil and from hydrocarbons or emulsifiers that are added to many preparations Symptoms are specific to the type of essential oil. Contact poisons information for advice if specific ingestant is known For 24 hour advice, contact the Poisons Information Centre 13 11 26
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Essential_Oil_Poisoning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Symptoms (including rapid CNS effects) usually start within one hour.** ⚠️ Aspiration signs are usually immediate but **can be delayed up to 6 hours**; biochemical changes after large ingestions may take 10 hours.
claims.source_text: Following ingestion, onset of symptoms (including rapid onset of CNS symptoms) is usually within one hour. Signs of aspiration usually appear immediately, but can be delayed up to 6 hours. Biochemical abnormalities following large ingestions may take 10 hours to occur
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Essential_Oil_Poisoning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Concentrations range 1–20%.** 5–15 mL is likely toxic in adults; ⚠️ **2–3 mL of some oils has been associated with toxicity in children.**
claims.source_text: Essential oil concentrations range from 1-20%. Volumes of 5-15 mL are likely to cause toxicity in adults Smaller Ingestions of 2-3 mL of some essential oils have been associated with toxicity in children
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Essential_Oil_Poisoning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Assess:** all deliberate self-poisoning or significant accidental ingestion · any symptomatic child · **ingested dose over 5 mL** · any child whose developmental age does not fit accidental poisoning.
claims.source_text: All patients with deliberate self-poisoning or significant accidental ingestion Any symptomatic patient Ingested dose >5 mL Any patient whose developmental age is inconsistent with accidental poisoning as non-accidental poisoning should be considered
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Essential_Oil_Poisoning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **History:** the exact oil name and volume, the preparation type and % concentration, and co-ingestants such as paracetamol.
claims.source_text: Exact name of oil and amount/volume taken Preparation type and % concentration, co-ingestants, eg paracetamol
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Essential_Oil_Poisoning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Any change in mental state is significant.** CNS depression, vertigo, dizziness, ataxia, seizures · bradycardia, hypotension · aspiration (gagging, choking, persistent coughing).
claims.source_text: CNS: CNS depression (any change in mental state is significant), vertigo, dizziness, ataxia, seizures CVS: Bradycardia, hypotension Respiratory: Aspiration pneumonitis (gagging, choking, persistent coughing)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Essential_Oil_Poisoning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Clove: urgent discussion with a toxicologist.** Large ingestions can cause paracetamol-like hepatotoxicity, renal failure, DIC, inhalational pneumonitis and coma.
claims.source_text: Clove Requires urgent discussion with toxicologist Large ingestions can have hepatotoxicity similar to paracetamol poisoning, renal failure, DIC, inhalational pneumonitis, coma
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Essential_Oil_Poisoning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Pennyroyal: urgent discussion with a toxicologist.** GI symptoms, lethargy, agitation, dizziness, weakness; large ingestions can cause paracetamol-like hepatotoxicity, renal failure, DIC and coma.
claims.source_text: Pennyroyal Requires urgent discussion with toxicologist Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, lethargy, agitation, dizziness and weakness. Large ingestions can have hepatotoxicity similar to paracetamol poisoning, renal failure, DIC, coma
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Essential_Oil_Poisoning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Wintergreen (98% methyl salicylate): as little as 1–2 mL can be toxic** — nausea, vomiting, tinnitus, vertigo, hyperventilation, seizures. See salicylate poisoning.
claims.source_text: Wintergreen (98% Methyl Salicylate) Nausea, vomiting, tinnitus, vertigo, hyperventilation, seizures. A dose as small as 1-2 mL can be toxic (see Salicylates Poisoning)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Essential_Oil_Poisoning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Seizure-prone oils:** fennel (seizures, pulmonary oedema) · thuja (multiple tonic-clonic seizures) · wormwood (acidosis, renal failure, rhabdomyolysis, delirium, seizures).
claims.source_text: Fennel Nausea, vomiting, seizure activity, pulmonary oedema … Thuja (Wormwood plant of the cedar family) Multiple tonic-clonic seizures … Wormwood Acidosis, acute renal failure, respiratory acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, visual alterations, delirium, restlessness, paranoia, tremor, seizures
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Essential_Oil_Poisoning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Others:** lavender (CNS depression, ataxia, photosensitisation, contact dermatitis) · nutmeg (hallucinations, coma) · lemon myrtle (skin irritation and corrosion) · geranium (allergic contact cheilitis).
claims.source_text: Lavender CNS depression, ataxia, photosensitiser that promotes hyperpigmentation, contact dermatitis … Nutmeg hallucinations, coma … Lemon myrtle Skin irritation and corrosion … Geranium Allergic contact cheilitis
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Essential_Oil_Poisoning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Asymptomatic, small ingestion: usually no tests.** Consider CXR and blood gas for aspiration signs; **UEC and LFT for significant illness, large ingestions, or clove or pennyroyal**; paracetamol level in all intentional overdoses.
claims.source_text: Asymptomatic children with small ingestions do not usually require investigation In all children, consider: Chest X-ray and blood gas if signs of aspiration pneumonitis UEC and LFT in patient with significant illness, large ingestions or with clove oil/pennyroyal ingestions Paracetamol level in all intentional overdoses
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Essential_Oil_Poisoning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Aspiration pneumonitis is managed supportively** (oxygen, bronchodilators, NIV or intubation if severe). Fever is common — **withhold antibiotics until there is objective evidence of bacterial infection**; no corticosteroids or prophylactic antibiotics.
claims.source_text: Aspiration/chemical pneumonitis is managed supportively with oxygen and bronchodilators and may require non-invasive ventilation or intubation if severe Fever is common following aspiration with pneumonitis. Antibiotics should be withheld until there is objective evidence of bacterial infection. Corticosteroids and prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Essential_Oil_Poisoning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Charcoal is contraindicated** — aspiration risk, and essential oils are absorbed rapidly.
claims.source_text: Charcoal is contraindicated due to risk of aspiration and due to the fact essential oils are rapidly absorbed.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Essential_Oil_Poisoning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider NAC for significant clove oil, pennyroyal or halogenated hydrocarbon poisoning** — discuss with Poisons Information or a toxicologist.
claims.source_text: Specific treatments: Consider NAC for significant clove oil, pennyroyal or halogenated hydrocarbon poisoning, discuss with poisons/toxicologist
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Essential_Oil_Poisoning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Eyes:** routine irrigation, possibly longer for oily substances; ophthalmology review for persistent symptoms. **Skin:** wash with soapy water and treat any dermatitis.
claims.source_text: Eye irritation management: Routine eye irrigation, however may require a longer duration of irrigation (oily substances). Persistent eye symptoms should have ophthalmology review Dermal exposure: Decontaminate area with soapy water, symptomatically treat any dermatitis/skin irritation
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Essential_Oil_Poisoning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Enhanced elimination is ineffective; there is no antidote.**
claims.source_text: Enhance elimination: ineffective Antidote: Nil
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Essential_Oil_Poisoning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Asymptomatic after significant exposure (over 5 mL) with normal vital signs and GCS: observe 4 hours before discharge.** Respiratory or CNS symptoms: admit for longer observation ± supportive care.
claims.source_text: Asymptomatic children with significant exposure (>5 mL) and normal vital signs including GCS, should be observed for 4 hours post exposure before discharge Patients with respiratory or CNS symptoms should be admitted for a longer period of observation +/- supportive care.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Essential_Oil_Poisoning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider admission for all adolescents with an intentional overdose.**
claims.source_text: Admission should be considered for all adolescents with an intentional overdose
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Essential_Oil_Poisoning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Transfer for significant CNS depression, seizures or respiratory compromise** — these children usually need PICU.
claims.source_text: A child has significant CNS depression, seizures or respiratory compromise as these children usually require ongoing management in a paediatric intensive care unit
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Essential_Oil_Poisoning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Discharge:** normal GCS and observation complete. Adolescents with deliberate ingestion need a self-harm risk assessment and drug and alcohol assessment first.
claims.source_text: Normal GCS Period of observation as above … Prior to discharge, adolescents who present with deliberate ingestions need a risk assessment regarding the likelihood of further ingestions or other attempts to self-harm Assessment of other drug and alcohol use should also be undertaken
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Essential Oil Poisoning' (Last Updated July 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Essential_Oil_Poisoning/, retrieved 2026-09-23
